title: The language of signs and notices
subtitle: Trespassers will be prosecuted
summary: Understand the short, formal English of public signs and notices, and be able to explain what each one means in everyday words.

lesson.heading: Why signs sound so strange
lesson.text: Signs and notices in English use words and expressions that are rarely seen anywhere else. They are short, impersonal and often quite formal, with Latin-based verbs like **prosecute** and **prohibit** and passive forms like **must be purchased**. Learn to 'translate' them into everyday English.

examples.note: People who walk on this private land will be taken to court.

examples.text: **PLEASE REFRAIN FROM USING MOBILE PHONES IN THE AUDITORIUM**
examples.note: Please don't use mobile phones in the theatre or hall.
Get off here for Buckingham Palace - seen on a bus.

lesson.heading: On the street and on the road
rows: Get off here for Buckingham Palace.
There is no way out at the other end of this road for cars.
Buy a ticket and put it where it can easily be seen.
at a car park or parking bays
Cyclists should get off their bikes here.
at a dangerous place or a pedestrians-only area

lesson.heading: In shops, cafes and at the door
rows: You can buy lunch here now.
outside or in the window of a cafe
Please put the things you are buying here.
You may not enter without permission or if you do not work here.
Young people under 18 can only come in with an adult.
People who steal from this shop will be taken to court.

lesson.heading: In parks, at the zoo and by the water
rows: People who walk on this private land will be taken to court.
at the entrance to a farm or forest
You can be taken to court and made to pay 1,000 pounds for dropping rubbish.
in a park or on a beach
You are not allowed to feed the animals.
Only people with a special card giving permission may fish here.
What is in this packet is officially considered bad for your health.

lesson.heading: The key words
lesson.text: A small group of formal words does most of the work in British signs. Learn them and you can decode almost any notice.

examples.text: to **prosecute** = to bring a legal case against someone; a **penalty** = a punishment
a **trespasser** = someone who goes on private land without permission
to **refrain** (from) = not to do something; to **prohibit** = to forbid something
to **alight from** = to get off a means of public transport; to **dismount** = to get off a bicycle or horse
a **minor** = a young person under 18; a **vehicle** = a means of transport; an **auditorium** = a large place where an audience sits; a **purchase** = something which has been or is to be bought

lesson.heading: More notices you will meet
rows: in a shop or restaurant: the staff can speak English
at customs: for people who have no goods they must pay duty on
at a shop: the shop is closing down and wants to sell all its goods
at a sports or cultural event: you must have a ticket to come in
at a hotel: it is full; at a factory or shop: no jobs are available
for example at an escalator: if you have a dog with you, you must carry it

lesson.heading: Polite requests on notices
lesson.text: Notices that ask rather than order usually begin with **Please** and use **refrain from** + *-ing*, or a passive. They sound firm but not rude.

examples.text: **Please give up this seat to an elderly or disabled passenger.**
examples.note: seen on a train or bus
outside a house or at an estate agent's: there is a flat you can rent

lesson.text: Never copy sign English into ordinary speech. You say *Could you get off at the next stop?*, not ~~Please alight at the next stop~~.

exercises.prompt: Match each formal sign word with its meaning.

pairs.right: to bring a legal case against
something which has been or is to be bought
someone who goes on private land without permission

exercises.prompt: Match each formal sign word with its meaning.

pairs.right: to get off a means of public transport
to get off a bicycle or a horse
a large place where an audience sits
a young person under the age of 18

exercises.prompt: Where would you expect to see ALIGHT HERE FOR BUCKINGHAM PALACE?
exercises.explanation: Alight from = get off a means of public transport.

exercises.prompt: Where would you expect to see TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED?
options: at the entrance to private land such as a farm or forest
exercises.explanation: A trespasser goes on private land without permission.

exercises.prompt: Where would you expect to see PLEASE REFRAIN FROM USING MOBILE PHONES IN THE AUDITORIUM?
exercises.explanation: An auditorium is the large space where an audience sits.

exercises.prompt: PAY AND DISPLAY. What must you do?
options: Buy a ticket and put it where it can easily be seen.
Pay when you leave the car park.
Show your driving licence to the attendant.
Pay a penalty for parking here.
exercises.explanation: Display means put it where it is easy to see - this sign is found in car parks.

exercises.statement: CYCLISTS DISMOUNT means that cyclists should get off their bikes.
exercises.explanation: Correct - dismount is the formal word for getting off a bicycle or a horse.

exercises.statement: NO ADMISSION TO UNACCOMPANIED MINORS means that children may come in but adults may not.
exercises.explanation: It means young people under 18 can only come in if they are with an adult.

exercises.prompt: A cafe owner wants to say that the cafe is now open for breakfast. The notice reads: Breakfast now being ___.
exercises.explanation: Now being served is the usual formula on cafe and restaurant notices.

exercises.prompt: A shop owner wants people to know that the staff can speak Spanish. The notice reads: Spanish ___ here.
exercises.explanation: English spoken here / Spanish spoken here - a very common shop notice.

exercises.prompt: A shop owner wants to warn thieves that they will be taken to court. The notice reads: Shoplifters will be ___.
exercises.explanation: To prosecute = to bring a legal case against someone.

exercises.prompt: A shop owner wants to ask customers politely not to touch the goods. The notice reads: Please ___ from handling the goods.
exercises.explanation: Refrain from doing something = not do it. It is very formal and typical of notices.

exercises.prompt: A manager wants to stop people who do not work there from entering. The notice reads: No entry to ___ personnel.
exercises.explanation: Unauthorised personnel = people who do not have permission or do not work here.
